newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilian carrier sets sights on Mercosur.
newsitem.headline: Brazilian carrier sets sights on Mercosur.

text.p: Brazilian airline TAM, Latin America's fastest growing regional carrier, says it plans to use its successful "red carpet service" strategy to elbow in on the booming Mercosur business travel market.
"There is a huge potential for growth in business travel in Mercosur. I want to build up our presence in the South American air travel market," TAM President Rolim Amaro said in a news conference.

Until recently a domestic carrier that only offered services within Brazil, last month TAM paid $27 million for a controlling share of Lapsa, a small Paraguayan-based carrier, which Amaro hopes will help him build up a presence in the region.

Amaro said the value of Lapsa lay not in its three aging Boeing 727-300's, but in the new routes which will allow TAM to fly from Brazil to Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia and Paraguay. Rolim also plans to transform the airport at the Paraguayan capital of Asuncion into a hub for TAM's Mercosur operation.
He argues Asuncion is ideally located at the geographical heart of the region and aproximately halfway between its two main business centers: Buenos Aires and Sao Paulo.
"Asuncion is an ideal center for TAM because our Fokker-100 planes can operate at lower costs," he said.

Thirty-five years ago, when he founded the company as a small air taxi service outfit, he saw the opportunity to develop a niche transporting businessmen to and from Brazil's prosperous but still small towns in the country's vast hinterland.
A former small plane pilot, Rolim built up a fleet of Fokker-100s, which were low on maintenance and adecquate for the short runways available in the small airports in which they landed.
TAM offers premium service -- at a price. Travel agents say on average TAM charges 20 percent more than its competitors.
But Rolim says his clients don't mind paying the extra money in exchange for on-time service and comfort.
Higher prices have also guaranteed comfortable profit margins and exceptional results. "We will not give up our margins. We use profits to expand," he said.
TAM shares have outperformed the 52-share Bovespa index by 82 percent so far this year. Net profits for 1995 were 43.9 million reais, up 142.5 percent over 1994.
TAM is also the only Brazilian airline to consistently show increased earnings. Brazil's flag carrier Varig showed a loss of 7.1 million reais in 1995 against a profit of 2.08 million reais 1994.
Rolim said plans for the future include the purchase of an Airbus Industrie Airbus 340 or a Boeing Co 747 to use the Lapsa routes to Europe and the United States.
